text:
B: Hiya, can you hear me alright?
A: Yes, I can hear you. Good afternoon. I am Tomasz.
B: Haider. Nice to meet you, Tomasz.
A: Nice to meet you. I saw your photo. You have the technical books, the network cables.
B: Ha, yeah, that shelf's a mess, to be fair. I do IT at a college in west London. Network, Wi-Fi, all that.
A: It is good work. Every place needs it now.
B: Yeah, true. What about you?
A: I was a civil engineer, drainage and highways design. Now I am looking for work. I was made redundant last year.
B: Ah, sorry, mate. That's tough. Is it going alright, the looking?
A: Slowly. I apply for many, and mostly they do not reply. But I keep trying. I am fifty-eight, so, er, it is not so easy maybe.
B: Nah, I get you. But engineers, they always need them, right? Roads, drains, it's not going anywhere.
A: That is what I say to my wife. The water will always need to go somewhere.
B: Ha, that's a good line, that. The book on my shelf, the CCNP, I've been meaning to study it for over a year. Keep putting it off. You sort of make me feel guilty now.
A: In my experience, er, the book does not read itself. Thirty minutes each evening, it is enough. That is how I did my CPD courses after work.
B: Thirty minutes. Yeah. That's doable, to be fair. I'll try that.
A: May I ask, the instrument in the corner of your photo. What is it?
B: Oh, that's an oud. It was my dad's. He passed away in 2016. I can play about three songs on it, badly.
A: I am sorry about your father. Mine also died, in 2015. In Poland. I could not get there in time.
B: Ah, man. I'm sorry. That's hard.
A: Yes. It was hard.
B: Yeah.
A: But it is good you keep the oud. And you play it. Three songs is not nothing.
B: Ha, nah, I suppose not. My mum likes it when I play, even when I mess it up. Where's home for you, then, in Poland?
A: Gdańsk. By the sea. And you, you are from London?
B: Sort of. Born in Baghdad, came here when I was thirteen. Hanwell now, with my mum and my brother.
A: Thirteen. So you are, er, how do you say, from both places.
B: Yeah, that's it. Both, and sometimes not enough of either, depending who's asking. You probably know that feeling.
A: Yes. Twenty years here, and in Gdańsk my sister still says I speak Polish like an Englishman.
B: Ha! My cousins in Baghdad said exactly the same thing about my Arabic. They were laughing at me the whole time we—
